quotes.text: AI doesn't clean up confusion by itself. It can search across more files, summarize more records and send a recommendation in seconds. But it also moves bad data faster.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States why governance has to come before AI automation.

quotes.text: Simply explained, it's a shared business dictionary with pre-approved calculations baked right in. You define a term once, store the logic once and reuse it everywhere
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A plain-language definition of a semantic layer.

quotes.text: Psychological safety means you can speak up without paying a social price for it. You can ask, where did this number come from? You can admit you don't fully understand a metric.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Connects psychological safety directly to data work.

quotes.text: Conflict doesn't break a data transformation. Avoiding conflict breaks it. Good conflict tests whether a claim can survive real questions.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A counterintuitive, memorable claim about healthy challenge.

quotes.text: Human in the loop sounds reassuring, but it only works when the human has real power to change the outcome. A rubber stamp at the end of an automated chain isn't judgment.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Defines what meaningful human oversight of AI requires.

chapters.title: Why faster AI answers still stall decisions

takeaways: AI moves bad data faster, so governance with named owners, sources and access rules has to come before automation.
A semantic layer gives humans and AI one shared definition of business terms, and every report should start from a named decision and decision owner.
Data transformation needs psychological safety to challenge the numbers and a named person who owns the final judgment on every AI-supported decision.
hook: Many organizations have Copilot, Power BI and Fabric, yet decisions still stall because nobody trusts the numbers or owns the call. This episode gives data and business leaders five pillars, from governance to human judgment, to test any report, prompt or flow before the next AI rollout.
